Consonantal i

Consonantal u

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

whereas conjunction

contrasting two facts

also while (contrasting), whilst (contrasting), on the other hand

classical

Cic. Sen. 17: cum aliī mālōs scandant, … ille autem clāvum tenēns quiētus sedeat in puppī

cum (+ subjunctive)

conjunction, with the subjunctive; the main clause often has autem or tamen

whereas, while

Adversative cum: the clause states the fact the main clause is set against. Often Latin needs no conjunction at all: it puts the two clauses side by side and sets their first words against each other (illī … hī), with at or autem in the second.

Other words

  • at, autem (in the second clause) — whereas, but on the other hand

    conjunctions; autem after the first word · also used · classical · Liv. 1.7.1: tempore illī praeceptō, at hī numerō avium rēgnum trahēbant; Gell. 13.24.2: vitiō vertunt, quia multa egeō; at ego illīs, quia nequeunt egēre

    The English “whereas” clause becomes a main clause with the contrasting word first.

  • contrā — on the other hand, on the contrary

    adverb · also used · classical · Traupman 325

    Sets a contrary statement against the last: sunt autem aliī philosophī quī contrā … (Plaut., Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • cum aliī mālōs scandant, aliī per forōs cursent, aliī sentīnam exhauriant, ille autem clāvum tenēns quiētus sedeat in puppī

    while some climb the masts, others run along the gangways and others bail out the bilge, he sits quietly in the stern holding the tillerCic. Sen. 17

  • tempore illī praeceptō, at hī numerō avium rēgnum trahēbant

    the one side claimed the kingdom by being first, whereas the other claimed it by the number of birdsLiv. 1.7.1

  • vitiō vertunt, quia multa egeō; at ego illīs, quia nequeunt egēre

    they find fault with me because I go without many things, whereas I find fault with them because they cannot go withoutGell. 13.24.2

See also but, while, however.
